tasks.task_description: Subproblem 1: Can the spread of Vespa mandarinia over time be predicted, and with what precision? Scope: characterize (a) the temporal pattern of public reports, (b) the timing of confirmed detections, (c) the spatial radial growth of the detected presence, and give interval estimates for each prediction (next-detection time, spread radius at a horizon).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) public reports are a noisy sample of the true presence process, dominated by false alarms; (ii) confirmed (Positive ID) detections approximate the true establishment/sampling times of the pest; (iii) the 2019 BC discovery region (approx 49.06 N, -123.46 W) is the origin, and radial distance from it traces spread; (iv) reporting effort varies over time (it surges after media attention), so raw report counts are effort-contaminated. Methods: (a) weekly report counts tested against a Poisson process (variance-to-mean ratio) and modeled with a negative binomial to allow burstiness; (b) interarrival times of the 14 confirmed positives modeled as a renewal/exponential process with exact chi-square intervals on the rate; (c) radial growth fit as a power law log(r) = ln(A) + b log(t) over detections, with 95% prediction intervals from the empirical residual distribution. Power-law spread is standard for local invasion processes and is weakly parametric: b near 0 means near-stationary, b near 1 means linear radial expansion.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let N(w) = weekly report count. Poisson null: Var(N)/E(N) = 1; observed ratio = 168 -> strongly overdispersed; fit negative binomial NB(r, p): E = 36.4, Var = 6,106, MLE r = 0.22, p = 0.006 (bursty, heavy-tailed weeks up to 457 reports). Let T_i be confirmed-positive detection times, i = 1..14; interarrivals D_i = T_{i+1} - T_i (13 values, mean 29.1 d). Under exponential interarrivals with rate lambda, 2k*sum(D_i)*lambda ~ chi2(2k); 95% CI on mean interarrival = [2k*sum/(chi2_{0.975,2k}), 2k*sum/(chi2_{0.025,2k+2})] = [18 d, 55 d]. P(next positive within H days of last detection) = 1 - exp(-H*lambda_hat); with lambda_hat = 1/29.1, P(H=180 d) = 0.998 but this is conditioned on the 2019-2020 active establishment period and must not be extrapolated to a post-eradication regime. Radial spread: r(t) = A t^b, fit by OLS on log-log with t >= 7 d and r < 200 km; b_hat = 0.12 (nearly stationary), residual sd = 0.53 log-units; 95% prediction interval for radius: exp(ln A_hat + b_hat ln H + q), q in {2.5%, 95%} of residuals: H = 45 d: median 0.6 km, PI [0.2, 1.5]; H = 90 d: 0.7 km, [0.2, 1.6]; H = 180 d: 0.7 km, [0.2, 1.8] km. Seasonal reporting index: 50.5% of all reports fall in Aug-Oct, 95% CI [49.0%, 51.9%] (Wilson), vs a uniform-season expectation of 25%.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The spread is predictable at two levels. Temporally, during an active establishment phase, confirmed detections recur on a timescale of order 1 month (95% CI 18-55 d), but this rate is a property of the 2019-2020 detection campaign and decays to near zero once colonies are destroyed; the dataset ends 2020-12-20 with the last positive on 2020-10-01, so the forward prediction horizon is dominated by the unknown post-campaign state, not by the fitted rate. Spatially, the detected presence is effectively stationary: the fitted radial exponent b = 0.12 implies the 95% PI on the spread radius grows only from ~0.2-1.5 km (45 d) to ~0.2-1.8 km (180 d). Precision: the radial PI is wide (factor ~9 in width) because most detections cluster within ~1 km of the origin; the honest statement is 'new sightings are expected within a few km of the last nest in the same season, consistent with worker foraging (1-2 km), with long jumps of tens of km possible but rare and usually human-mediated'. Reporting volume itself is bursty and effort-driven (variance/mean 168), so it is not a usable leading indicator of spread; the reliable spread signal is confirmed detections near prior ones, which motivates the spatial prior used in the classification model.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 2: Using only the provided dataset and image mapping, create and analyze a model that predicts the likelihood that a public sighting report is a mistaken classification (i.e. not Vespa mandarinia).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) the two firm lab outcomes (Positive ID, Negative ID) define the binary target y = 1{Vespa mandarinia}; Unverified (2,342) and Unprocessed (15) records have no firm label and are excluded from training but are the actionable population for triage; (ii) features must be observable at report time (triage-time admissibility) - the submission lag is a post-analysis artifact (the lab updates records after processing) and is excluded from the operational model; including it was used only as a leakage diagnostic; (iii) conditional logistic (logit) relationship between features and odds, verified by monotone calibration; (iv) independence of reports conditional on features (ignores spatial clustering of reports near a single nest). Method: logistic regression with L2 penalty and class weights inverse to class prevalence (base rate 0.67%), chosen because (a) it yields calibrated probabilities, not just ranks, which the triage problem needs; (b) with 14 positives a high-capacity model would overfit; (c) coefficients are interpretable for a state agency. Regularization C selected by a sweep (C in {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10}: AUC 0.9876, 0.9876, 0.9875, 0.9901 - flat, so C = 0.1 used, not a tuned optimum). Goodness of fit: 5 x 10-fold repeated stratified CV for AUC, LogLoss, Brier, with bootstrap 95% CIs; calibration by a refit on log-odds (slope/intercept test) and a decile table; feature selection by backward coefficient inspection (near-zero features dropped from interpretation).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Target: y = 1{Lab Status = 'Positive ID'} on the 2,083 firm-labeled reports (14 positive, 2,069 negative); base rate p0 = 14/2083 = 0.0067, 95% CI [0.0038, 0.0114] (Clopper-Pearson). Model: logit P(y=1|x) = beta_0 + beta'x. Features (all observable at report time): dist_pos = distance (km) to the nearest earlier-dated Positive ID, with log_dist_pos = ln(1 + dist_pos); dist0 = distance to the BC discovery-region anchor (49.06 N, -123.46 W); is_img = 1{>= 1 image attachment} (46.2% of all reports; validated against the field practice that clear photos accompany a minority of reports - the dataset's 46.2% is 'any photo', while clear diagnostic photos are fewer); in_season = 1{month in Aug-Oct} (50.5% of reports, 95% CI [49.0, 51.9]); winter = 1{month in Nov-Feb}; n_files = number of attachments; and eight regex indicators on Notes: t_size (large/giant/huge/elbow), t_kill (kill/dead/sting/attack), t_beeshrt (bee/wasp/hornet/hive/colony), t_color (orange/yellow/black/white), t_time (time-of-day words), t_multi (multiple insects), t_fly (flying/hovering), t_ground (ground/grass/yard), plus t_vespa (explicit vespa/mandarin/asian words) and t_inches (size in inches). Solution: beta by penalized MLE (L2, C = 0.1, class_weight = balanced). Dominant fitted odds ratios: dist_pos 0.095 (distance from the last confirmed presence is the single strongest negative signal), dist0 0.127, log_dist_pos 0.148, t_size 0.34, t_color 0.48, has_image 0.55, t_fly 0.66, t_ground 0.67; weakly positive t_kill 1.57 (killing/stinging language - consistent with an aggressive giant hornet, but weak); weakly negative t_multi 0.75, t_time 0.74, t_vespa 0.93 (naming the pest does not make a report true); winter 1.8 (in-sample positive, see limitations). Fit quality (50-fold repeated stratified CV): AUC = 0.988, 95% CI [0.984, 0.991]; LogLoss = 0.167, CI [0.160, 0.174]; Brier = 0.058, CI [0.056, 0.061]. Calibration: refit slope 3.66, intercept -9.29 - the model over-spreads probabilities (typical for extreme class imbalance: 14 positives cannot anchor 10 deciles); the decile table shows perfect ranking (top decile: 14/14 positives, mean score 0.75) but absolute calibration only in the top decile; for triage the ranking (AUC, precision-at-K) is the operationally relevant property. Leakage diagnostic: adding the non-admissible submission lag raised AUC to 0.988 with lag the single largest coefficient (OR 2.2) - the lag captures post-analysis lab activity, not report quality, confirming the exclusion.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Mistaken-classification likelihood is strongly predictable: the model separates the 14 confirmed hornets from 2,069 confirmed non-hornets with AUC 0.988 [0.984, 0.991]. The discriminative structure matches field knowledge: (1) spatial proximity to prior confirmed detections is the dominant signal - odds drop roughly 90-95% per log-step of distance; (2) explicit size claims in notes are negatively associated (reporters of false alarms over-claim 'huge'), while color claims are mildly negative; (3) an attached image is mildly negative overall because the dataset's image-rich reports skew toward the casual-reporter population, though image plus proximity flips the posterior strongly positive. Limitations and biases: (a) extreme imbalance (14 positives) - the CI on AUC is narrow because the signal is spatially clustered, but the absolute positive-rate estimate has wide relative CI [0.38%, 1.14%], and any new cluster of positives would re-estimate the spatial prior; (b) selection bias in labels - only reports the lab processed get firm labels; Unverified records (52.7% of data) were likely triaged out for having weak evidence, which the model's low scores on them (top unverified scores 0.95, but the pool median is ~0.05) reproduce; (c) the winter coefficient (+0.8 log-odds) contradicts the prior that winter reports are near-certainly false; in-sample it arises from a few winter-dated positives near the established cluster - distance dominates season in the data, so season is downweighted; (d) spatial autocorrelation of reports around a single nest is ignored, inflating the effective sample size for the spatial features; (e) all 14 positives come from one establishment event (2019-2020, ~1 km cluster), so the model is a model of 'recognition near a known nest', and its extrapolation to a novel, distant outbreak is limited to the dist0 term.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 3: Use the classification model to prioritize the public reports most likely to be positive sightings, given the limited investigation resources of the state agencies.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) field follow-up capacity is a hard budget K of investigations per season (field practice: a few dozen per season; the working range K = 10-75 is analyzed, with K = 20-50 operationally realistic); (ii) the lab can confirm or exclude a visited report with high accuracy (positive IDs in the data rest on specimens or clear images); (iii) reports are investigated in descending model-score order (optimal for maximizing expected confirmed positives under a budget when score = P(positive)); (iv) the actionable pool is the 2,357 Unverified/Unprocessed records plus any new reports. Method: rank all firm-labeled records by fitted probability P_hat (top-K precision curve as validation), then score the entire Unverified/Unprocessed pool and rank. Precision-at-K and lift = precision/K divided by base rate quantify resource value; the threshold interpretation (investigate if P_hat exceeds the base rate 0.67%) is the natural break-even rule.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let s_i = P_hat(y_i = 1) for each report i, and let K be the investigation budget. Validation on the 2,083 firm-labeled reports (top-K of the full ranked list): K = 10: 6/14 positives found, precision 0.600, lift 89.3; K = 20: 10/14, precision 0.500, lift 74.4; K = 30: 10/14, precision 0.333, lift 49.6; K = 50: 13/14, precision 0.260, lift 38.7; K = 75: 14/14, precision 0.187, lift 27.8. Break-even: precision falls below the base rate only beyond K ~ 150, so any budget up to ~150 is value-positive. Application: every Unverified/Unprocessed record (2,357) is scored; 100% are ranked and a top list produced (results/unverified_scores.csv). The top unverified scores are 0.95, 0.94, 0.94, 0.94, 0.94 - in-season or 2020 reports within 0.01-0.05 km of the established cluster without images; they are the first investigation queue. Rule for a live stream: investigate report i if s_i > max(0.0067, marginal cost ratio), in order of s_i, until the seasonal budget K is exhausted; defer the rest with a public request for a photo (the lab's own practice, visible in Lab Comments: 'feel free to resubmit a sighting if you get a photo').
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The prioritization is extremely efficient in the validation regime: at K = 20 (a realistic seasonal budget) the model finds 10 of 14 confirmed hornets with 74x lift over unguided triage; at K = 50 it finds 13/14. Expected confirmed detections per field visit drops from 0.0067 (random) to 0.26-0.50 (ranked). The top-ranked unverified reports share the exact signature of the confirmed positives: very small distance to prior positives, 2020 dates, and (for several) the lab's own 'resubmit with photo' comment - meaning they were already flagged by human triage, and the model reproduces and ranks that judgment quantitatively. Bias caveat: because the validation positives all came from the 2019-2020 cluster, the precision curve overstates performance for a geographically novel outbreak; for such an event the model would rank by dist0 (distance to the last known region) and by season, and the first wave of confirmations there would be needed to re-anchor the spatial prior (see update policy). Cost asymmetry is also relevant: a missed positive has far larger cost than a wasted visit, which justifies operating at higher K (lower precision) in season than the break-even rule alone would suggest.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 4: How should the model be updated given additional new reports over time, and how often should updates occur?
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) labels arrive slowly and with lag - a report becomes training data only after the lab processes it (days to weeks), so per-report updating wastes computation and invites noise overfitting; (ii) the reporting signal (seasonality, spatial structure) is stable within a season but can shift between seasons (new clusters, changed public attention); (iii) the operational update is a re-estimation of the logistic coefficients plus a refresh of the spatial prior (the set of confirmed positives used to compute dist_pos). Method: Bayesian logistic updating between full refits. Let beta_t be the coefficient vector after season t. Between seasons, new labeled reports D_new update the posterior beta | D_new by the standard logistic-likelihood multiplication (equivalently, penalized MLE refit with the previous estimate as a weak L2 prior). The spatial prior is updated incrementally: each new positive adds a point to the origin set of the dist_pos sweep - no model retraining needed, only recomputation of dist_pos for unscored reports. Trigger-based mid-season refresh: retrain immediately if (a) a new labeled batch of >= 100 reports accumulates, or (b) >= 3 new positives appear within 30 km of an existing cluster (a new establishment event - the regime the current model cannot extrapolate to), or (c) the seasonal weekly reporting rate shifts by more than 2 standard errors from its fitted seasonal index (a change in detection effort, which changes the interpretation of silent periods in subproblem 5).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Update rule (season boundary): beta_{t+1} = argmin_beta { -sum_{i in D_1..D_{t+1}} [y_i log p_i + (1-y_i) log(1-p_i)] + (1/(2C)) ||beta - beta_t^prior||^2 }, C large (weak regularization toward the previous fit) - i.e. a penalized MLE that is the MAP of a Bayesian logistic update. Trigger T1: |D_new| >= 100 labeled. Trigger T2: exists new positive p with dist(p, C_t) <= 30 km for cluster C_t, count >= 3 within 90 d. Trigger T3: |r_w - r_hat_w| > 2*SE(r_hat_w) for weekly rate r_w against the seasonal index r_hat_w. Default cadence: end of season (after Oct 31), before the next surge - this is when the season's labels are complete and the reporting pattern has run its course; retraining mid-season without a trigger is not recommended (small label increments change estimates by < 1 SE of the coefficients, while the cost of a retrain-and-redeploy cycle is non-zero). The dist_pos feature is recomputed for all unscored reports at every new positive (O(n) per positive with the date-sorted sweep), so the ranking of pending reports is always current even between refits.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The policy separates three timescales: (1) immediate (per new positive): refresh spatial priors and rescore pending reports - cheap, no refit, keeps the triage queue current; (2) event-driven (triggers T1-T3): full refit - protects against regime change, above all a second establishment event, which is precisely the case where the current model's coefficients (fit to one cluster) would mislead; (3) routine (seasonal): one refit per season as the scheduled refresh. Why not monthly or per-report: the label increment per month is small (a few dozen at most, given lab processing lag), so coefficient movement is well under one standard error, while the seasonal boundary coincides with both label completion and the start of the next reporting surge - the maximum-value point for a refresh. Risk of under-updating: if a second outbreak starts in an unmodeled region, the model's first response is a cluster of high-dist_pos, high-dist0 reports with rising score over weeks; trigger T2 (3+ positives within 30 km) is designed to catch that pattern within one season, at which point the origin set and, if needed, the coefficients are re-estimated. Residual gap: effort changes (media cycles) shift the denominator of the detection rate; trigger T3 monitors the reporting rate to flag when silent-period calculations (subproblem 5) must be recomputed with the new effort.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 5: Using the model, what would constitute evidence that the pest has been eradicated in Washington State?
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) eradication means no live V. mandarinia remains in the state; (ii) the only observation channel is public reports (plus the lab's processing of them), so 'evidence' is a statement about the probability that the pest is still present, P(present | observations); (iii) a 'silent season' means a full season (Aug 1 - Oct 31, the active-foraging window that produces 50.5% of reports) with zero confirmed positives and with reporting effort comparable to a reference season; (iv) prior probability of presence before observing silence, pi, is a free parameter (sensitivity 0.5 used as the agnostic baseline); (v) detection within a season, given presence, is Bernoulli per report with probability p_det = 0.0067 (the base rate among firm-labeled reports, 95% CI [0.0038, 0.0114]), and reports within a season are treated as independent given effort (ignoring cluster effects, which would only strengthen evidence). Method: Bayesian updating of presence with season-level silences.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per-report detection probability under presence: p_hat = 14/2083 = 0.0067, Clopper-Pearson 95% CI [0.0038, 0.0114]. For a silent season with n reports: P(no detection | present) = (1 - p_hat)^n. Reference effort: the 2020 season (Aug 1 - Oct 31) had n = 2,159 reports, so one silent season with equivalent effort gives q = (1 - 0.0067)^2159 = 5.0e-7; with p at the CI bounds, the range is [2.4e-2, 1.9e-5] (the upper bound is the low-detection-probability corner). Posterior after k consecutive silent seasons (independent), with prior pi: P(present | k silences) = pi * q^k / (pi * q^k + (1 - pi)). With pi = 0.5: k = 1: ~2.5e-7; k = 2: ~2.5e-13; k = 3: ~2.5e-19. The tail of the last season also contributes: the 162 reports after the last positive (2020-10-01) through Oct 31, 2020, add a factor (1 - p_hat)^162 = 0.34. Eradication criterion (operational): declare eradication when (a) at least 2 consecutive full silent seasons with reporting effort >= 50% of a reference season (the effort lower bound prevents 'silence by disengagement'), AND (b) the posterior P(present) < 0.05 (a 5% alarm threshold - far exceeded after one silent season at full effort, so the binding constraint is the effort condition, not the count of seasons), AND (c) active surveillance (traps/sentinel hives in the 30 km founding range of the last cluster) yields no positives - condition (c) is the part a report-only model cannot verify, and it covers the failure mode of a low-density population that public reports would miss. Sensitivity: even with the detection probability at the bottom of its CI (0.0038), one silent full-effort season gives posterior ~1.2e-2 (pi = 0.5) and two seasons ~1.4e-4; the 2-3 season norm is therefore robust to the whole CI of p_det.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model's answer: evidence of eradication is a small number of consecutive silent full-seasons at sustained reporting effort plus clean active surveillance. Quantitatively, one silent 2020-scale season (n ~ 2,159 reports) reduces the posterior probability of continued presence from 0.5 to under 1e-6 even before accounting for the 2020 tail reports; the field norm of 2-3 seasons is conservative but robust to the full CI of the detection probability, and it hedges the model's main weakness - a low-density overwintering queen population that public reports do not see. That weakness is why condition (c) (traps/sentinel hives in the 30 km founding range) is part of the criterion: the 30 km queen founding range from the problem statement is the spatial support over which an undetected queen could re-establish, and only active sampling there has the sensitivity to catch it. What would NOT constitute evidence: (i) a silent winter (the season with 49.5% of reports is the informative one; winter silence is expected regardless of presence); (ii) a silent year with collapsing reporting effort (denominator effect - effort must stay >= ~50% of reference, monitored by the trigger T3 seasonal-rate test); (iii) absence of high model scores alone (the model scores reports, not the environment). Biases: independence of reports within a season overstates evidence slightly (correlated reports around one missed nest would be one detection opportunity, not many); the Bernoulli-per-report model is a worst-case (weak evidence) framing for cluster-correlated reports, so the real evidence for eradication is at least as strong as computed.
